title: Clinical Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Care
description: Pharmaceutical care process, patient counselling and adherence, therapeutic drug monitoring, clinical pharmacokinetics, and pharmacist roles in chronic disease management.

topics.title: Pharmaceutical Care and Medication Review
topics.summary: The pharmaceutical care process, drug therapy problems and care plans.

notes.b: Pharmaceutical care (Hepler and Strand, 1990) is the responsible provision of drug therapy to achieve definite outcomes that improve a patient's quality of life. The patient care process: collect (medication history — including herbal and over-the-counter products, which are widely used in Nigeria — allergies, comorbidities, laboratory data), assess (identify drug therapy problems), plan (goals, interventions, monitoring), implement and follow up. The seven drug therapy problem categories (Cipolle, Strand, Morley): unnecessary drug therapy, needs additional drug therapy, ineffective drug, dosage too low, adverse drug reaction, dosage too high, and non-adherence. Documentation (e.g. SOAP notes — Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) and communication with prescribers are essential. Medication review (clinical medication review, medicines use review) is especially valuable in polypharmacy and older adults.
k: Collect, assess, plan, implement, follow up

notes.b: Clinical pharmacists participate in ward rounds, medication reconciliation at admission, transfer and discharge, prescription screening and interventions, therapeutic drug monitoring, antimicrobial stewardship, anticoagulation clinics, parenteral nutrition, drug information and patient counselling. In Nigeria, clinical pharmacy is growing with the Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD) programme (introduced from 2016 to prepare pharmacists for patient-oriented roles), the West African Postgraduate College of Pharmacists fellowship, and pharmacist-led clinics (HIV, hypertension, diabetes). Evidence shows pharmacist interventions reduce medication errors, adverse drug events, readmissions and costs. Interprofessional collaboration and respectful communication (e.g. SBAR — Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) improve acceptance of recommendations.

topics.title: Patient Counselling and Adherence
topics.summary: Counselling techniques, health literacy, adherence assessment and interventions.

notes.b: Effective counselling covers the medicine's name and purpose, dose, how and when to take it (with or without food), duration, expected benefits, common and serious side effects and what to do, interactions (including food, alcohol and herbs), storage, and what to do if a dose is missed. Techniques: open-ended questions (e.g. the Indian Health Service 'prime questions': What did your doctor tell you the medicine is for? How did the doctor tell you to take it? What did the doctor tell you to expect?), the teach-back method (the patient explains in their own words), demonstration (inhalers, insulin pens, eye drops), and written information or pictograms. Consider health literacy, language (English, Pidgin, Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo), culture, beliefs about medicines, and privacy. Counselling for special devices: metered-dose inhalers (shake, exhale, seal lips, press and inhale slowly, hold breath ~10 seconds; spacers improve delivery), insulin (injection sites rotation, storage in the fridge or cool pots), and oral rehydration salts preparation.
k: Name, purpose, dose, duration, side effects

notes.b: Adherence is the extent to which a patient's behaviour matches agreed recommendations; about 50% of patients with chronic diseases do not take medicines as prescribed (WHO). Factors (WHO five dimensions): socioeconomic (cost — out-of-pocket payments in Nigeria, distance), health system (stock-outs, poor communication), condition-related (asymptomatic diseases like hypertension), therapy-related (complex regimens, side effects, pill burden) and patient-related (beliefs, forgetfulness, stigma — e.g. HIV). Assessment: self-report questionnaires (Morisky scale), pill counts, pharmacy refill records, electronic monitors and drug levels (e.g. viral load in HIV). Interventions: simplify regimens (once-daily fixed-dose combinations), address costs (health insurance, generics), reminders (SMS, alarms), adherence counselling, community refill and multi-month dispensing, treatment supporters, and addressing beliefs and stigma. Intentional non-adherence (deciding not to take) differs from unintentional (forgetting).

topics.title: Clinical Pharmacokinetics and TDM
topics.summary: Key PK parameters, dosing calculations, and therapeutic drug monitoring of narrow-range drugs.

notes.b: Key parameters: bioavailability (F — fraction reaching systemic circulation; IV = 100%), volume of distribution (Vd = amount in body / plasma concentration — determines loading dose: LD = Cp target × Vd / F), clearance (CL — volume cleared per unit time — determines maintenance dose: MD rate = CL × Css / F), half-life (t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL), and elimination rate constant. Steady state is reached after about 4–5 half-lives (regardless of dose); a loading dose achieves target concentrations sooner. First-order kinetics: a constant fraction is eliminated per unit time; zero-order (saturable) kinetics: a constant amount — phenytoin, ethanol, high-dose aspirin — small dose increases cause large level rises. Renal impairment reduces clearance of renally excreted drugs (aminoglycosides, vancomycin, digoxin, lithium) — estimate creatinine clearance (Cockcroft–Gault) and adjust doses or intervals. Hepatic impairment, age, obesity, pregnancy and critical illness alter pharmacokinetics.

TDM is useful for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, poor dose–response predictability, and a measurable concentration–effect relationship: aminoglycosides (gentamicin — once-daily dosing with trough levels < 1 mg/L to minimise nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; peak relates to efficacy), vancomycin (trough or AUC-guided dosing — nephrotoxicity), digoxin (0.5–2.0 ng/mL; sample at least 6 hours post-dose; toxicity — nausea, visual disturbances, arrhythmias, worsened by hypokalaemia), lithium (0.4–1.0 mmol/L; sample 12 hours post-dose), phenytoin (10–20 mg/L; adjust for low albumin), theophylline (10–20 mg/L), carbamazepine, ciclosporin and tacrolimus (transplant). Correct sampling time relative to dose and at steady state is essential; interpret levels with clinical status. Limited TDM availability in Nigerian hospitals means clinical monitoring (renal function, symptoms, ECG) is often relied upon.

topics.title: Pharmaceutical Care in Chronic Diseases
topics.summary: Hypertension, diabetes, asthma/COPD, HIV and anticoagulation management by pharmacists.

notes.b: Hypertension: pharmacists screen blood pressure, confirm diagnosis with repeat readings, counsel on lifestyle (salt reduction — seasoning cubes are a major source in Nigeria), optimise regimens (CCB or thiazide first-line in black patients, add ACEi/ARB; single-pill combinations), monitor potassium and creatinine with ACEi/ARB and diuretics, and follow up to target. Diabetes: glucose monitoring education (glucometer technique, targets), metformin counselling (with meals, GI effects), sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia recognition and management, insulin technique and storage (refrigerate unopened; in-use pens at room temperature up to 28 days; clay pot coolers where electricity is unreliable), foot care, and cardiovascular risk reduction (statins, BP). Dyslipidaemia: statins (take simvastatin at night; myopathy — report muscle pain; interactions with clarithromycin). Heart failure: daily weights, salt restriction, diuretic adjustment and adherence to guideline therapy.

Asthma/COPD: inhaler technique (errors are very common), distinguishing relievers from preventers, adherence to inhaled corticosteroids, asthma action plans, smoking cessation, spacer use and vaccination. HIV: adherence counselling, managing side effects, drug interactions (rifampicin with dolutegravir — double DTG dose; antacids/iron/calcium chelate dolutegravir — take DTG 2 hours before or 6 hours after; efavirenz with hormonal contraceptives), differentiated service delivery (community pharmacy ART refill). Anticoagulation: warfarin (INR target 2–3 for most indications; 2.5–3.5 for mechanical mitral valves; many interactions — antibiotics, antifungals, herbal products; consistent vitamin K intake — green leafy vegetables; bleeding signs), direct oral anticoagulants (fewer interactions, no routine INR, adjust for renal function). Pharmacist-managed anticoagulation clinics improve time in therapeutic range.

topics.title: Special Populations and Clinical Nutrition
topics.summary: Paediatric and geriatric pharmacotherapy, pregnancy and lactation, renal and hepatic impairment, and parenteral nutrition.

notes.b: Paediatrics: dose by weight (mg/kg) or body surface area; suitable formulations (dispersible tablets, suspensions); avoid aspirin (Reye's syndrome), tetracyclines (teeth), fluoroquinolones in general (cartilage — used when benefits outweigh risks), chloramphenicol in neonates (grey baby syndrome), and codeine in children under 12. Geriatrics: altered pharmacokinetics (reduced renal clearance, increased body fat), increased sensitivity (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics), polypharmacy and falls — deprescribing, Beers and STOPP/START criteria. Pregnancy: use drugs with established safety (paracetamol, methyldopa, nifedipine, labetalol, insulin, penicillins); avoid teratogens (ACE inhibitors, warfarin in the first trimester, valproate, isotretinoin, tetracyclines, methotrexate). Lactation: most drugs are compatible; consider infant exposure (e.g. avoid codeine in ultra-rapid metabolisers). Renal impairment: adjust renally cleared drugs, avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast). Hepatic impairment: reduce doses of highly metabolised drugs, avoid hepatotoxins, caution with sedatives (encephalopathy).

Nutrition support is needed for malnourished patients or those unable to eat. Enteral nutrition (oral supplements, nasogastric or gastrostomy feeding) is preferred when the gut works — it maintains gut integrity and is cheaper and safer. Parenteral nutrition (PN) is used when the gut cannot be used (intestinal failure, severe short bowel, prolonged ileus); components: dextrose (carbohydrate), amino acids, lipid emulsions (essential fatty acids), electrolytes, vitamins, trace elements and water — compounded aseptically in pharmacy (all-in-one 'three-in-one' bags) with attention to stability (calcium–phosphate precipitation, lipid emulsion stability). Peripheral PN requires osmolarity < about 900 mOsm/L; higher needs a central line. Complications: catheter-related bloodstream infection, hyperglycaemia, refeeding syndrome (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia — start slowly, give thiamine), liver dysfunction and electrolyte imbalance. Energy requirements are about 25–30 kcal/kg/day and protein 0.8–1.5 g/kg/day (higher in critical illness).
